newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sainsbury goes for quality as profits slip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sainsbury goes for quality as profits slip.

text.p: British supermarket group J. Sainsbury Plc reined in its pursuit of arch-rival Tesco on Wednesday after reporting a 15 percent fall in annual profits but an apparent gain in sales momentum.
"I am not setting market share leadership as a goal (on its own)...I will not go blindly to market share at any price," chief executive Dino Adriano told journalists at a news conference.
"Being the biggest is not necessarily the same as being the best," he added.
Sainsbury, smarting from its eviction from top slot among British supermarkets by Tesco over a year ago, has been striving to reassert itself amid accusations of complacency.

The supermarket chain said that latest year pretax profits before exceptional items totalled 651 million pounds ($1.1 billion) in the 52 weeks to March 8, down from 764 million previously but marginally better than the 640-650 million it forecast in January.
The group paid out a dividend of 12.3 pence per share compared with 12.1 pence, where some analysts had been expecting no change.

It said that same store sales in the seven weeks since the start of the new financial year were up by 4.2 percent, compared with a rise of four percent in the 16 weeks to January 11, although over the key Christmas period sales were up 4.4 percent.
"The tide has turned. Our like-for-like sales are rising while others are falling," Adriano told Reuters.

Sainsbury stunned the market and sent its shares tumbling in January when it warned that the costs of pushing sales forward would hurt, with profits falling for only the second time in its history as a public company.

When Tesco reported in April a 10 percent rise in annual profits to 750 million pounds, it said current sales growth from existing stores was about six percent, down from 7.5 percent gains registered at Christmas.
Adriano emphasised that Sainsbury's figures represented real volume growth of 2.5 percent as inflation was running at around 1.5 percent.
Sainsbury's shares jumped to a high of 360 pence but later eased back to be up five pence at 351 pence by 1300 GMT.
"The really good news is that there seems to be a recovery in the core business, but there is no reason to get excited," said Bill Myers, analyst at Williams de Broe.
Chairman David Sainsbury said in a statement with the results that "in the year ahead we are focused on sustaining higher sales momentum and translating this into satisfactory profit growth."
Adriano said the group's Reward loyalty card had had a "major impact" on sales but its costs had held back gross margins, which were stable last year and are expected to continue steady.
"Our great hope is that we can at least achieve stable margins, we'd like to do better," he said.

Sainsbury was forced into the embarrassing U-turn of launching Reward last year after Tesco's sales stormed ahead on the back of its ClubCard scheme, which David Sainsbury had dismissed when it was launched.

Sainsbury said operating margins slipped to 6.2 percent last year, partly through costs of the launch of Reward and a fierce petrol price war, which together cost the supermarkets some 38 million pounds.
Sainsbury estimated that Reward, which gives customers points to offset against future purchases and special offers, is used for 80 percent of sales.

Adriano said the company wanted to maintain the momentum in sales and bring in new customers, with an advertising campaign focusing on "Fresh food, fresh ideas" to be launched in the next couple of weeks.

"We've got (momentum) going. We're not stopping at this point, we've got the new advertising campaign...a lot of other developments coming through...we intend to build, and build, on what we have clearly started," he said.

Sainsbury said supply chain improvements should see cost savings of 50 million pounds over the next three years, while working on converting computer software to cope with the date change in 2000 would cost the group 40 million, with half of that incurred in the current year.
The group said it also hoped for "significant improvement" in operating profits at its Homebase do-it-yourself business and Shaw's in the U.S. after heavy investment.
In Northern Ireland, Adriano said the group aims to grow organically from its current two stores but did not rule out "the odd store" being bought.
Tesco spent 630 million pounds in March buying the Irish supermarkets of Associated British Foods (ABF).
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
